title: Barrage of earthquakes suddenly strike Los Angeles
text:

Dozens of earthquakes struck Southern California on Saturday — with a major cluster concentrated in South Los Angeles.

The sudden burst included a 2.7-magnitude quake in Westmont around 2:30 a.m. Saturday, followed by a 2.6-magnitude temblor in the same area around 4:30 p.m., according to the US Geological survey

More than 60 quakes in total hit the area, with many coming in at under magnitude 2.0.

Farther out, a pair of earthquakes were recorded southeast of Catalina Island within minutes of each other just before 4:15 a.m.

The surge occurred as a 3.4-magnitude quake struck in the Bay Area overnight Saturday, and after a 3.2-magnitude tremor rattled South Los Angeles less than a week ago.

The burst comes as a new study reignited concerns over the San Andreas Fault that runs through California, with experts warning the catastrophic “Big One” may strike sooner than previously thought.

Saturday, September 12, 2026, 3:55 PM: There have now been over 70 small earthquakes in the Lennox, California region in the last 24 hours. I’m watching this swarm very closely as it crosses over the Newport-Inglewood Fault. #CAwx #earthquake #LosAngeles pic.twitter.com/ULa3VEk7gP

Caltech seismologist Dr. Lucy Jones warns the disaster would be far more than a brief jolt, as her models show it would unleash widespread, devastating impacts across the state.

Meanwhile, researchers at the University of California, Riverside say they have developed a way to identify the most likely locations of some of the world’s biggest quakes.

They add the approach works by determining where stress has been building along major fault lines, which can help pinpoint where a major earthquake is most likely to occur.

The researchers focus on regions called subduction zones — areas where one tectonic plate slides beneath another.

These zones tend to produce the world’s biggest earthquakes, including those measuring magnitude 8.5 or greater.
